literal: An edict handed the matter to the Eight Seats for deliberation, specially granting leniency, stripping rank and removing office.
idiomatic: The throne referred the case to the Eight Seats; Kuang was specially pardoned, stripped of his title, and dismissed from office.

literal: Langzhong of the Three Ducal Offices Xin Xiong memorialized to settle the case.
idiomatic: Langzhong Xin Xiong of the Three Ducal Offices submitted a memorial to adjudicate the matter.

literal: Later specially appointed Inspector of Ping Province, transferred to Inspector of Qing Province, soon made Commander-in-Chief of the Pass West, concurrent with the touring secretariat of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He was later made inspector of Ping, then of Qing, and soon commander-in-chief of Pass West with a concurrent Masters of Writing field staff.

literal: Encountering illness he returned to the capital.
idiomatic: Illness brought him back to the capital.

literal: At the beginning of Xiaochang he died; posthumous title: Wen Zhen.
idiomatic: He died early in Xiaochang and was posthumously styled Wen Zhen.

literal: Later his original rank was posthumously restored and he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Jinan.
idiomatic: Later his original title was restored posthumously and he was re-created prince of Jinan.

literal: His fourth son Xian succeeded.
idiomatic: The fourth son, Xian, inherited.

literal: When Qi received the Mandate, titles were reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: After Qi took the throne, enfeoffments were lowered by precedent.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: Wei shu juan 19a: in the tables of contents of various editions this scroll is noted "deficient."
idiomatic: Every edition's table of contents marks Wei shu juan 19a as "lacunose."

literal: The Bai nang edition, Southern edition, Ji edition, and Bureau edition at this scroll's end have a Song editor's note saying: "Wei Shou's book, Biographies of the Twelve Princes of Jingmu, scroll upper—is lost.
idiomatic: Bai nang, Southern, Ji, and Bureau editions end with a Song note: "Wei Shou's scroll of Jingmu Twelve Princes, upper volume, is lost.

literal: " The Palace edition's textual verification says: "Wei Shou's book is lost; later people supplemented it.
idiomatic: " The Palace Kaozheng adds: "Wei Shou's text is lost; later hands filled it in.

literal: " Commentary: This biography was supplemented from Beishi juan 17, Biographies of the Twelve Princes of Jingmu; now and then there are superfluous words and sentences that must come from the Gaoshi xiaoshi.
idiomatic: " Note: This life was patched from Beishi juan 17 (Jingmu Twelve Princes); stray phrases occasionally must come from Gaoshi xiaoshi.

literal: The Shizong, first year of Jingming, died in office as Inspector of Qing Province. In various editions "yuan" (first) is written "liu" (six); the Palace edition has "yuan."
idiomatic: "Died as Qing inspector in Shizong Jingming year 1": most editions read yuan (1) as liu (6); the Palace text has yuan.

literal: Beishi juan 17: the Bai nang edition lacks this character; other editions sometimes have "six."
idiomatic: Beishi juan 17: Bai nang lacks the character; other witnesses read "six."

literal: Commentary: Jingming has no sixth year; Yi died in the eleventh month of Jingming year 1, as seen in juan 8, Annals of Shizong; now follow the Palace edition.
idiomatic: Note: Jingming had no year 6; Yi died eleventh month, Jingming 1 (juan 8, Shizong annals); the Palace reading is adopted.

literal: Posthumous title: Wen. Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Cong
idiomatic: "Posthumous title Wen": Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Cong

literal: 〈plate 100〉
idiomatic: plate 100

literal: It says: "Posthumous title: Wen Jing."
idiomatic: reads: "Posthumous title Wen Jing."

literal: " Epitaph and biography posthumous titles differ in many cases; sometimes the epitaph records a title and the biography lacks it, sometimes the biography records one and the epitaph lacks it.
idiomatic: " Epitaphs and lives often disagree on posthumous styles; sometimes the stele records a title the biography omits, sometimes the reverse.

literal: Some are changed posthumous titles before and after; some are original titles not handsome, privately altered by descendants; some are later supplemented titles—not only epitaph and biography differ, epitaphs with epitaphs also often disagree; it is very hard to judge right and wrong.
idiomatic: Some reflect later renamings, some ugly originals privately softened by heirs, some belated supplements—not only stele against biography but stele against stele; right and wrong are hard to settle.

literal: Henceforth whenever posthumous titles differ or are present or absent, all will not be noted in collation.
idiomatic: Hereafter posthumous variants will not be recorded in collation notes.

literal: Transferred to Inspector of Ji Province. From this sentence down to the passage below "transferred to Right Bearer of the Bright Insignia"—a paragraph absent from Beishi juan 17.
idiomatic: "Made inspector of Ji": from here through "made Right Bearer of the Bright Insignia" Beishi juan 17 has no parallel.

literal: Commentary: Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Yao
idiomatic: Note: Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Yao

literal: 〈plate 106〉
idiomatic: plate 106

literal: Says that in Jingming times he "went out invested as General Who Stabilizes the Army and Inspector of Ji Province, entered dismissed as Guardian of the Army, added as Right Bearer of the Bright Insignia."
idiomatic: says that in Jingming he "went out as general stabilizing the army and Ji inspector, came in as guardian of the army with the added rank of right Bearer of the Bright Insignia."

literal: In Yanzhou times, Huai and Si were not quiet; added as General Who Pacifies the South and Commander of the Southern Campaign armies."
idiomatic: In Yanzhou, with trouble on Huai and Si, he was further named general pacifying the south and commander of southern campaign armies."

literal: Then Yao as Inspector of Ji Province was in Yuan Ke's Jingming years;
idiomatic: So Yao's tenure as Ji inspector fell in Yuan Ke's Jingming era;

literal: He was from Inspector of Ji Province entering as Right Bearer of the Bright Insignia and Guardian of the Army—not as this biography says, with Left Bearer of the Bright Insignia, holding Guardian of the Army, going out as Ji Province; even less at "the beginning of Suzong."
idiomatic: he entered from Ji as right Bearer of the Bright Insignia and guardian of the army—not, as this life has it, as left Bearer leading the guard and then going out to Ji, and certainly not at "the beginning of Suzong."

literal: This paragraph was probably taken by whoever supplemented this biography from the Gaoshi xiaoshi or another book, mistaking the chronology, thereby inverting before and after.
idiomatic: The interpolator likely lifted this block from Gaoshi xiaoshi or another source, botched the dates, and reversed the sequence.

literal: Below it again says "transferred to Right Bearer of the Bright Insignia"—in fact a repetition of the earlier "Left Bearer of the Bright Insignia"
idiomatic: The later line "transferred to Right Bearer of the Bright Insignia" merely repeats the earlier "Left Bearer of the Bright Insignia"

literal: 〈Beishi already errs in making "right" into "left"〉
idiomatic: Beishi already corrupts you (right) to zuo (left)

literal: , and the traces of insertion are very clear.
idiomatic: —the seam of interpolation is obvious.

literal: Memorial requesting to change name to Zhi. Commentary: Above it says "Yao's younger brother Heng"; then this person's original name was Heng, later changed to Zhi.
idiomatic: "Memorial to rename Zhi": above calls him "Yao's younger brother Heng"—so his original name was Heng, later Zhi.

literal: According to juan 8, Annals of Shizong, eighth month of Zhenshi year 3 one sees "Yuan Heng"; while juan 9, Annals of Suzong, sixth month bingzi of Xiaochang year 2, first month jiashen of Xiaochang year 3, juan 10, Annals of Xiaozhuang, fourth month jihai of Wutai year 1, and juan 58, Biography of Yang Chun—all see "Yuan Heng Zhi."
idiomatic: Shizong annals, juan 8, Zhenshi 3.8, cite Yuan Heng; Suzong annals (juan 9), Xiaochang 2.6 bingzi and 3.1 jiashen, Xiaozhuang annals (juan 10) Wutai 1.4 jihai, and Yang Chun's biography (juan 58) cite Yuan Heng Zhi.

literal: It is suspected the original name was "Heng," later adding the character "Zhi."
idiomatic: He probably began as Heng and later added the character Zhi.

literal: Prince of Runan Tiansi enfeoffed in third year of Heping. Commentary: Tiansi on day wuyin, seventh month of Heping year 2, together with Xiaoxincheng and Wanshou received enfeoffment on the same day, as seen in juan 5, Annals of Gaozong; here "three" should be the corruption of "two."
idiomatic: "Prince of Runan Tiansi enfeoffed Heping 3": juan 5 (Gaozong) has wuyin day, seventh month, Heping 2, when he was enfeoffed with Xiaoxincheng and Wanshou—here "3" corrupts "2."

literal: Below, the biography of Prince of Yuele Wanshou has the same error.
idiomatic: The life of Prince Wanshou of Yuele below repeats the error.

literal: Gaozu valued him. In various editions "zu" (ancestor) is written "zong" (ancestor/emperor); Beishi juan 17 has "Xiaowen."
idiomatic: "Gaozu valued him": editions read zu as zong; Beishi juan 17 has Xiaowen.

literal: Commentary: Yuan Kuang is Yuan Jun's
idiomatic: Note: Yuan Kuang was Yuan Jun's

literal: 〈Gaozong〉
idiomatic: Gaozong

literal: younger brother Xincheng's son; if here it read "Gaozong," then below Yuan Jun calls him "paternal uncle"—would it not be inverted?
idiomatic: younger brother Xincheng's son; calling him Gaozong here would make Yuan Jun's "paternal uncle" below nonsensical.

literal: Beishi has "Xiaowen"; whoever supplemented this biography following Wei shu usage changed it to "Gaozu"; "zu" corrupted to "zong"; now corrected.
idiomatic: Beishi reads Xiaowen; the patcher, following Wei shu style, wrote Gaozu; zu corrupted to zong—now restored.

literal: And the Master of Writing Ling minister Zhao, on Fang's fabrication
idiomatic: But Minister Ling Zhao of the Masters of Writing, on Fang's measure

literal: 〈to〉
idiomatic: to (lacunose)

literal: still said Fu. Commentary: This paragraph's meaning cannot be understood.
idiomatic: still said Fu. Note: This passage will not parse.

literal: Below "fabrication" and below "Fu" there must be missing text.
idiomatic: Text is missing after zao (fabrication) and after Fu.

literal: Yi in the center has nothing. Zhang Senkai's Beishi collation notes say: "It is suspected yi (restrain) is the error of zhe (break/fold)."
idiomatic: "Yi in the center has nothing": Zhang Senkai's Beishi collation (suspected yi corrupts zhe).

literal: " Commentary: Tongzhi juan 84 lower correctly has "zhe"; the suspicion is probably correct.
idiomatic: " Note: Tongzhi juan 84 lower reads zhe; the emendation is likely right.

literal: Fear this comes from the heart. Zhang Senkai says: "It is suspected ci (this) should be the character fei (not); written as ci it does not match the text's meaning."
idiomatic: "Fear this comes from the heart": Zhang Senkai suspects ci (this) should be fei (not)—ci will not parse.

literal: Liu Fang's learning was high for the age and deeply versed in classical precedent; what he relied on compared with the Former Dynasty's foot-rule—yet the inch exceeded by one millet—how could one again say it was the Former Dynasty's intent? Commentary: Above one praises Liu Fang; below one should not say what he relied on did not match the "Former Dynasty foot-rule" and so on.
idiomatic: The passage praises Liu Fang's learning yet faults his standard against the "former-dynasty foot" while calling the inch one millet too long and still invoking court intent—after praising Fang, the censure of his measure against the "former-dynasty foot" is incoherent.

literal: According to Wang Xian's impeachment memorial above, it says "Fang's fabricated inch stops at only ten millet"; then the so-called "inch exceeding by one millet" clearly is not denouncing Fang—probably it points to the foot-rule Yuan Kuang fabricated.
idiomatic: Wang Xian's memorial above says Fang's inch used exactly ten millet; "one millet too long" therefore targets Kuang's rule, not Fang's.

literal: Here below "what he relied on" there must be missing text.
idiomatic: Text is missing after "what he relied on."

literal: Probably it means Liu Fang relied on the foot-rule promulgated by the "Former Dynasty," while what Yuan Kuang fabricated had "the inch exceeding by one millet"; hence below denouncing Yuan Kuang "what he held was uncanonical."
idiomatic: Likely Fang followed the court's former promulgated foot, whereas Kuang's inch ran one millet long—hence the later charge that Kuang's standard was uncanonical.

literal: Now at "what he relied on" below, the sentence is broken off.
idiomatic: The sentence is broken after "what he relied on."

literal: Privately succeeding for many years. Commentary: Above the text clearly says Yuan Ke
idiomatic: "Privately succeeding for many years": above Yuan Ke is named

literal: 〈Shizong〉
idiomatic: Shizong

literal: at that time, Kuang had already requested to succeed the enfeoffment of Shaoluohou, passed through the Masters of Writing deliberation and memorialized to inherit the enfeoffment—then it was not at all private succession, and moreover inheritance of the enfeoffment had been long.
idiomatic: when Kuang had already petitioned to inherit Shaoluohou, the Masters of Writing deliberated and memorialized the succession—hardly a private adoption, and long settled.

literal: One does not know why before and after contradict.
idiomatic: Why the account contradicts itself is unclear.
